Ethanolamine-mediated microstructural transitions within terpenoid- and fatty acid-based deep eutectic solvents†
Anjali and Siddharth Pandey (ID) *

Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have emerged as solubilizing media of intense interest due partly to their easily tailorable physicochemical properties. Extensive H-bonding between the constituents in a two-constituent system is the major driving force for the formation of the DES. Addition of ethanolamine (MEA), a compound having H-bonding capabilities, to the DESs composed of a terpene [menthol (Men) or thymol (Thy)] and a fatty acid [n-decanoic acid (DA)] results in an unprecedented increase in dynamic viscosity due to the extensive rearrangement in the H-bonding network and other interactions within the system, while the liquid mixture still behaves as a Newtonian fluid. For the non-DA DES constituted of Men and Thy, this behavior is not observed. Visual color appearance, density and electrical conductivity measurements, UV-Vis and FTIR absorbance, differential scanning calorimetry, and empirical Kamlet–Taft parameters of the MEA-added DA-based DESs reveal the microstructural changes effectively. Cybotactic regions of the fluorescent microfluidity probes [1,3-bis(1-pyrenyl)propane – an intramolecular excimer forming probe, as well as perylene and 1,6-diphenylhexatriene – well-established anisotropy probes] also manifest the unprecedented increase in the viscosity of the DA-based DES system upon MEA addition. The carboxylic acid functionality of the DA plays a crucial role in bringing microstructural changes within the system as MEA is added. Physicochemical properties of DES systems can be effectively manipulated by not only changing the constituents and their compositions, but also by judicious addition of a co-solute/co-solvent. This work offers an easy and efficient way to favorably tailor the properties of interest of these environmentally-benign media.

# 1. Introduction In recent decades, efforts have been invested by the scientific community in creating more cost-effective and environmentally-benign alternatives to conventional solvents that can exhibit novel and tunable solvating capabilities. 1,2 In this regard, deep eutectic solvents (DESs), usually formed from the combination of H-bond donor (HBD) and H-bond acceptor (HBA) moieties, have garnered considerable attention. 3-7 Their physicochemical attributes have been extensively documented in numerous publications in recent times.6-13 An important yet newer subset of the survey involves the exploration of "binary" mixtures, which include DESs as one of the components. Such a mixture consisting of a DES and a small functional molecule can introduce a new complexity to these media and can offer tunability to their existing physicochemical

While the effect of water has been extensively studied experimentally and computationally, 14-19 the interest is now shifting towards the potential offered by a mixture of DES with small organic functionalities.

By mixing a DES with a judiciously selected molecule having appropriate functionalities, not only can the physicochemical properties of the DES be tailored effectively but media having unusual properties may be obtained through disturbing/modifying the existing interactions between the HBD and HBA within the system. In this context, the knowledge of molecular-level microstructural transition within such media becomes of utmost importance. The primary objective of this work is to afford the microstructural transition within the "binary" mixtures of naturally-derived hydrophobic DESs (HDESs) and a small organic molecule, ethanolamine (MEA), which is a good H-bond donor as well as acceptor. MEA also facilitates the microemulsification of fatty acid-based DESs and water systems as documented in our previous research.20 There, the water solubility curve exhibited a Gaussian type

We have also identified an optimum concentration of MEA, which ensures a maximum water retention by the system. This unu- sual behavior has prompted us to investigate the microstruc- tural transition within these fatty acid-based DESs in the presence of MEA in a comprehensive manner.

Towards this end, we have selected three (3) DESs constituted of a saturated alkyl chain fatty acid (n-decanoic acid; DA) and two common terpenes (thymol; Thy and menthol; Men) in a molar ratio of 1:1, namely (DA:Thy), (DA:Men) and (Thy:Men). We investigated the impact of the addition of varying amounts of MEA (up to mole fraction 0.50) on their physicochemical properties. Dynamic viscosity measurements carried out initially within a temperature range 293 to 343 K show an unusual increase in viscosity upon MEA addition to DA-based DESs, whereas the viscosity change in the (Thy:Men) DES was as expected. The (DA:Thy) DES system has shown a more pronounced effect with MEA addition compared to the (DA:Men) and (Thy:Men) systems. Therefore, to obtain insight into the structural transitions, if any, within the MEA-added (DA:Thy) DES system, rheology, electrical conductivity, UV-vis as well as FTIR absorbance, and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) of this system were investigated. Furthermore, suitable optical spectroscopic probes were employed to obtain empirical Kam-let-Taft parameters of solvent polarity and H-bonding ability, and the microviscosity of the aforementioned systems was explored using a ratiometric intramolecular excimer forming fluorescent probe along with steady-state and time-resolved fluorescence anisotropy probes. This afforded insights into the microfluidity afforded by the MEA-added DES media to
solutes of importance and also revealed the correlation between the unusual increase in bulk viscosity with the probe-reported microviscosity within such interesting media.

## 2. Experimental ### 2.1. Materials Thymol (Thy; ≥99%), L-(-) menthol (Men; ≥99%), and n-decanoic acid (DA; ≥98%) were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and were stored in a desiccator. DESs were prepared by simply mixing the constituents in a 1:1 molar ratio followed by gentle heating and constant stirring until the mixture became clear and transparent. Ethanolamine (MEA; ≥99.5%) was purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and was stored under a highly inert atmosphere. Intramolecular excimer forming fluorescent probe 1,3-bis(1-pyrenyl)propane (BPP) was acquired from molecular probes in the highest purity. Fluorescence anisotropy probes, perylene and 1,6-diphenyl-1,3,5-hexatriene (DPH), were purchased from Sigma-Aldrich and Acros Organics, respectively. All the chemicals were used as received without any further purification and were stored in a desiccator. All the possible precautions were taken to protect the samples from moisture. While the structures of the DES constituents, Thy, Men, and DA, and the fluorescent microfluidity probes, BPP, perylene, and DPH, are presented in Fig. 1, details of the DES systems used are listed in Table S1 (ESI†).

## 3. Results Depending upon the nature and the extent of interactions present, the physicochemical properties of a multicomponent mixture may deviate from their ideal additive values estimated from those of the individual components. We have investigated MEA-added DES [(Thy:DA), (Men:DA), and (Thy:Men)] systems at MEA mole fraction ranging from 0 to 0.50 considering the (Thy:Men) system as the control system. The images of the MEA-added DES (Thy:DA) system are shown in Fig. 2. It is clear from the images that MEA induces color changes in the DA-based (Thy:DA) and (Men:DA) DESs within a particular MEA concentration range. For (Thy:DA), color is induced between 0.29 ≤ χMEA ≤ 0.44, while for (Men:DA), it starts appearing at a lower MEA concentration compared to (Thy:DA), and the color is also less strong in the (Men:DA) system. However, no color is observed in the (Thy:Men) DES upon MEA addition (all the samples remain transparent throughout the entire MEA composition range from 0 to 0.50). This is the first evidence of microstructural transformation that might be taking place in DA-based DESs upon MEA addition.

## 3.1. Variation in density upon MEA addition The densities of the MEA-added DES systems, [(Thy:DA)/MEA, (Men:DA)/MEA, (Thy:Men)/MEA], are measured in the temperature range of 293 to 343 K with the MEA composition ranging from 0 to 0.50 mole fraction. Fig. S1 (ESI†) shows the variations in density with the change in temperature and composition (the corresponding density values are presented in Table S2, ESI†). As expected, with increase in temperature, the density of the MEA-added DES systems decreases linearly (recovered R² ≥ 0.99) due to an increase in volume for all the investigated systems. The density of the MEA-added DES systems monotonically increases as more and more MEA is added, which is expected since MEA has a higher density (ρ = 1.01 g cm⁻³ at 298 K, for example) than the density of the neat DESs [for (Thy:DA), ρ = 0.930 g cm⁻³; for (Men:DA), ρ = 0.896 g cm⁻³; and for (Thy:Men), ρ = 0.933 g cm⁻³ at 298 K]. ## 3.2. Effect of MEA addition on dynamic viscosity An interesting trend is observed in the dynamic viscosity (η) of the investigated DES systems as MEA is incrementally added. Careful examination of Fig. 3 and entries in Table S3 (ESI†) reveals an interesting outcome. The η of MEA at 293 K is 24.08 (±0.05) mPa s. For each of the DES systems, η increases monotonically as MEA is added, with the

### 3.3. Temperature dependence of dynamic viscosity As expected, dynamic viscosity decreases monotonically with increasing temperature for each system (Table S3, ESI† and Fig. 4). The Vogel-Fulcher-Tammann (VFT) model²⁴ has shown better correlation between η and T in the temperature range of
293 to 343 K rather than the Arrhenius model: $\text{ln }\eta = A + \frac{B}{T - T_0}$ (4)

where A and B are empirical parameters, and T₀ is the fixed temperature where the configurational entropy of the system completely vanishes. Temperature dependence of the viscosity is fitted to the VFT equation and the recovered parameters are reported in Table S6 (ESI†) along with the goodness-of-fit in terms of R². The R² further validates the good adherence to the VFT model for all the systems investigated here (plot of ln η vs. T⁻¹ is shown in Fig. 4 along with the best fit curves). The activation energy of the viscous flow (Eₐ,η) at 298 K is calculated from the recovered parameters according to the expression:
$$E_{a,\eta} = RB\left(\frac{T}{T-T_0}\right)^2 \quad (5)$$

It is interestingly to note the trends in Ea,η among the MEA-added DES systems (Table S6, ESI†). The Ea,η of neat MEA is 34.3 (±1.8) kJ mol⁻¹. While the Ea,η values of (Thy:DA) and (Men:DA) are fairly similar in magnitude [31.1 (±1.8) and 35.5 (±2.0) kJ mol⁻¹, respectively], for (Thy:Men) the Ea,η is much higher [60.2 (±2.9) kJ mol⁻¹] suggesting interactions to be different when MEA is added to this DES as opposed to DA-based DESs. This further corroborates the MEA composition dependent η data discussed in the previous section. Interestingly, addition of MEA does not result in any significant changes in the Ea,η of the (Thy:Men) system, whereas for DA-based DESs, the Ea,η increases significantly [to 66.2 and 55.5 kJ mol⁻¹ for (Thy:DA) and (Men:DA), respectively, for 0.5 mole fraction MEA addition]. Clearly, addition of MEA brings considerable changes within the DA-based DES systems as opposed to (Thy:Men) DES – the presence of a carboxylic acid group on a DES constituent plays a critical role (vide supra). For DA-based DESs, an almost linear increase in Ea,η with increase in MEA mole fraction hints at the presence of stronger intermolecular H-bonding interactions between the DES and MEA as compared to interactions within the DES and within MEA, respectively.

## 4. Discussion The anomalously high viscosity of terpenoid containing DA-based DESs upon addition of MEA is the most interesting aspect of this work considering no gel-phase is formed as clearly implied by the rheology measurements. The viscosity of the MEA-added DA-based DES systems is observed to even surpass the viscosity of the neat components – DES and MEA – at all the investigated compositions and temperatures, which is a rarely observed phenomenon. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report documenting such viscosity ‘synergism’ involving DES systems. Similar behavior has primarily been observed in a few non-DES systems previously. For instance, viscosity synergism has been reported for ionic liquids mixed with polymers, such as [emim][OTf] + PEG MMA (6.2 ethoxy units in PEG) and [emim][BF₄] + PEG DMA (9 ethoxy units in PEG) at 40 °C, as well as for [bmim][PF₆] + PEG systems (PEG 200, 400, 600, and 1000) at specific temperatures and compositions.³⁹ Viscosity synergism in aqueous mixtures is reported for short-chain alcohols,⁴⁰ dimethyl sulfoxide,⁴¹ hydroxypropyl-substituted guar and carboxymethyl hydroxypropyl-substituted guar,⁴² acetone,⁴³ and isobutyric acid,⁴⁴ while in non-aqueous systems, it has been observed in only a few systems, such as (methanol + chloroform),⁴⁵ (o-chlorophenol + dioxane),⁴⁶ (carbon tetrachloride + ethyl acMEAte),⁴⁷ (dimethyl sulfoxide + acetic acid),⁴⁶ and (methanol + toluene).⁴⁷ The rarity of viscosity synergism within non-aqueous systems underscores the novelty of the current findings.

There are circumstantial pieces of evidence suggesting that even a slight modification in HBD and HBA constituents of DES can result in drastic alteration in their physicochemical proper- ties, and hence, their interactions with other moieties.6,19,48 In the present investigation, drastic alterations are induced by MEA as an additive that significantly perturbs the existing H-bonding network of the DES. Among the major alterations, a pronounced synergistic viscosity effect is observed in long chain fatty acid (i.e., DA) based DESs in contrast to those DESs that do not have carboxylic acid as a constituent. hypothesize that an extensive H-bonding between DES and MEA involving the carboxylic acid functionality of DA could be one of the possible reasons for the observed synergistic effect in all the investigated systems. This hypothesis is duly supported by the observation that (ln η)ᴱ decreases as tempera- ture increases. Typically, this trend is observed in H-bonded systems where H-bond strength weakens as the temperature rises. FTIR absorbance data also supports this hypothesis suggesting that extended H-bonding is responsible for the synergistic effect in viscosity.

However, based on electrical conductivity and UV-vis absorbance data, it appears that in MEA-added DA-based DESS, the synergistic viscosity effect is not solely due to the formation of an extended H-bonding network, additional factors, such as induced ionic interactions, also contribute significantly in bringing out synergism. Due to the confluence of various factors, the system exhibits a divergence point (χMEA ~ 0.3) beyond which viscosity and electrical conductivity experiences an exponential rise. FTIR absorbance has been highly instrumental in determining the extent of chemical and physical interactions present within the systems; for example, MEA-added (Thy:DA) has much higher chemical activity as compared to MEA-added (Thy:Men). Specifically, physical interactions are evident by subtle changes in the bending and stretching frequencies of various functional groups, such as, C=C, C-O, NH2, -OH, etc., upon addition of MEA. This implies the presence of strong physical interactions, H-bonding in particular. Chemical interactions are strongly detected in the stretching frequency of the carbonyl peak of DA along with the electrical conductivity and UV-vis absorbance data. Additionally, formation of new fluxional bonds or entities is further supported by the strong exothermic events at lower temperatures in the DSC profile of MEA-added DES systems, further supporting the presence of chemical interactions. Interestingly, ratio of excimer-to-monomer emission intensity of BPP and steady-state (perylene) and time-resolved (perylene and DPH) anisotropy measurements suggest that chemically-driven bulk viscosity mirror images the local cybotactic region viscosity (i.e., microviscosity) sensed by the solute probes. The MEA-added (Thy:DA) DES systems exhibit both physicochemical changes and induced ionic interactions that result in higher and unexpected viscosity in comparison to the MEA-added (Thy:Men) DES system, which demonstrates only physical interactions albeit weaker in comparison.

## 5. Conclusion The H-bonding and other interactions within DESs constituted of carboxylic acid as a constituent can be effectively manipulated and altered by addition of a judiciously selected external species. MEA, capable of readily forming H-bonding, when added to (Thy/Men:DA) DESs not only significantly alters the H-bonding network, but also creates induced ionic interactions within the DES system. These major microstructural changes amply get manifested in an anomalous increase in the viscosity

and electrical conductivity of the system – both these properties attain unusually high values that are much higher than that of the neat DES and neat MEA. The MEA-added DA-based DESs behave as Newtonian fluids thus discarding the possibility of gel formation within the system. The appearance of color upon MEA addition to DA-based DESs hints at the possible presence of larger aggregates due to H-bonding and induced ionic interactions, which is further supported by significant altera- tions in the IR absorbance bands and the emergence of new bands perhaps due to the formation of fluxional bonds. Solute cybotactic region viscosity (microviscosity) mirrors the bulk dynamic viscosity, further supporting the above reasons for the physicochemical changes within the MEA-added DA-based DES systems. The work put-forth an effective way of modulating the properties of DESs by addition of judiciously selected additives without altering the DES constituents and composi- tion. The outcome widens the application potential of DESs and further enhances their utility as new-age environmentally- benign inexpensive bio-derived solubilizing media.

Temperature dependence of dynamic viscosity As expected, dynamic viscosity decreases monotonically with increasing temperature for each system (Table S3, ESI† and Fig. 4). The Vogel-Fulcher-Tammann (VFT) model²⁴ has shown better correlation between η and T in the temperature range of 293 to 343 K rather than the Arrhenius model: $\text{ln }\eta = A + \frac{B}{T - T_0}$ (4) where A and B are empirical parameters, and T₀ is the fixed temperature where the configurational entropy of the system completely vanishes. Temperature dependence of the viscosity is fitted to the VFT equation and the recovered parameters are reported in Table S6 (ESI†) along with the goodness-of-fit in terms of R². The R² further validates the good adherence to the VFT model for all the systems investigated here (plot of ln η vs. T⁻¹ is shown in Fig. 4 along with the best fit curves). The activation energy of the viscous flow (Eₐ,η) at 298 K is calculated from the recovered parameters according to the expression: $$E_{a,\eta} = RB\left(\frac{T}{T-T_0}\right)^2 \quad (5)$$ It is interestingly to note the trends in Ea,η among the MEA-added DES systems (Table S6, ESI†). While the Ea,η values of (Thy:DA) and (Men:DA) are fairly similar in magnitude [31.1 (±1.8) and 35.5 (±2.0) kJ mol⁻¹, respectively], for (Thy:Men) the Ea,η is much higher [60.2 (±2.9) kJ mol⁻¹] suggesting interactions to be different when MEA is added to this DES as opposed to DA-based DESs. Interestingly, addition of MEA does not result in any significant changes in the Ea,η of the (Thy:Men) system, whereas for DA-based DESs, the Ea,η increases significantly [to 66.2 and 55.5 kJ mol⁻¹ for (Thy:DA) and (Men:DA), respectively, for 0.5 mole fraction MEA addition]. Discussion The anomalously high viscosity of terpenoid containing DA-based DESs upon addition of MEA is the most interesting aspect of this work considering no gel-phase is formed as clearly implied by the rheology measurements. The viscosity of the MEA-added DA-based DES systems is observed to even surpass the viscosity of the neat components – DES and MEA – at all the investigated compositions and temperatures, which is a rarely observed phenomenon. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report documenting such viscosity ‘synergism’ involving DES systems. Similar behavior has primarily been observed in a few non-DES systems previously. For instance, viscosity synergism has been reported for ionic liquids mixed with polymers, such as [emim][OTf] + PEG MMA (6.2 ethoxy units in PEG) and [emim][BF₄] + PEG DMA (9 ethoxy units in PEG) at 40 °C, as well as for [bmim][PF₆] + PEG systems (PEG 200, 400, 600, and 1000) at specific temperatures and compositions.³⁹ Viscosity synergism in aqueous mixtures is reported for short-chain alcohols,⁴⁰ dimethyl sulfoxide,⁴¹ hydroxypropyl-substituted guar and carboxymethyl hydroxypropyl-substituted guar,⁴² acetone,⁴³ and isobutyric acid,⁴⁴ while in non-aqueous systems, it has been observed in only a few systems, such as (methanol + chloroform),⁴⁵ (o-chlorophenol + dioxane),⁴⁶ (carbon tetrachloride + ethyl acMEAte),⁴⁷ (dimethyl sulfoxide + acetic acid),⁴⁶ and (methanol + toluene).⁴⁷ The rarity of viscosity synergism within non-aqueous systems underscores the novelty of the current findings. There are circumstantial pieces of evidence suggesting that even a slight modification in HBD and HBA constituents of DES can result in drastic alteration in their physicochemical proper- ties, and hence, their interactions with other moieties.6,19,48 In the present investigation, drastic alterations are induced by MEA as an additive that significantly perturbs the existing H-bonding network of the DES. Among the major alterations, a pronounced synergistic viscosity effect is observed in long chain fatty acid (i.e., DA) based DESs in contrast to those DESs that do not have carboxylic acid as a constituent. FTIR absorbance has been highly instrumental in determining the extent of chemical and physical interactions present within the systems; for example, MEA-added (Thy:DA) has much higher chemical activity as compared to MEA-added (Thy:Men). Specifically, physical interactions are evident by subtle changes in the bending and stretching frequencies of various functional groups, such as, C=C, C-O, NH2, -OH, etc., upon addition of MEA. This implies the presence of strong physical interactions, H-bonding in particular. Chemical interactions are strongly detected in the stretching frequency of the carbonyl peak of DA along with the electrical conductivity and UV-vis absorbance data. Additionally, formation of new fluxional bonds or entities is further supported by the strong exothermic events at lower temperatures in the DSC profile of MEA-added DES systems, further supporting the presence of chemical interactions. Conclusion The H-bonding and other interactions within DESs constituted of carboxylic acid as a constituent can be effectively manipulated and altered by addition of a judiciously selected external species. MEA, capable of readily forming H-bonding, when added to (Thy/Men:DA) DESs not only significantly alters the H-bonding network, but also creates induced ionic interactions within the DES system. These major microstructural changes amply get manifested in an anomalous increase in the viscosity and electrical conductivity of the system – both these properties attain unusually high values that are much higher than that of the neat DES and neat MEA. The MEA-added DA-based DESs behave as Newtonian fluids thus discarding the possibility of gel formation within the system. The appearance of color upon MEA addition to DA-based DESs hints at the possible presence of larger aggregates due to H-bonding and induced ionic interactions, which is further supported by significant altera- tions in the IR absorbance bands and the emergence of new bands perhaps due to the formation of fluxional bonds. Solute cybotactic region viscosity (microviscosity) mirrors the bulk dynamic viscosity, further supporting the above reasons for the physicochemical changes within the MEA-added DA-based DES systems. The work put-forth an effective way of modulating the properties of DESs by addition of judiciously selected additives without altering the DES constituents and composi- tion. The outcome widens the application potential of DESs and further enhances their utility as new-age environmentally- benign inexpensive bio-derived solubilizing media. Phys., 2025, 27, 3124 Ethanolamine-mediated microstructural transitions within terpenoid- and fatty acid-based deep eutectic solvents† Anjali and Siddharth Pandey (ID) * Deep eutectic solvents (DESs) have emerged as solubilizing media of intense interest due partly to their easily tailorable physicochemical properties. Extensive H-bonding between the constituents in a two-constituent system is the major driving force for the formation of the DES. Addition of ethanolamine (MEA), a compound having H-bonding capabilities, to the DESs composed of a terpene [menthol (Men) or thymol (Thy)] and a fatty acid [n-decanoic acid (DA)] results in an unprecedented increase in dynamic viscosity due to the extensive rearrangement in the H-bonding network and other interactions within the system, while the liquid mixture still behaves as a Newtonian fluid. For the non-DA DES constituted of Men and Thy, this behavior is not observed. Visual color appearance, density and electrical conductivity measurements, UV-Vis and FTIR absorbance, differential scanning calorimetry, and empirical Kamlet–Taft parameters of the MEA-added DA-based DESs reveal the microstructural changes effectively. Cybotactic regions of the fluorescent microfluidity probes [1,3-bis(1-pyrenyl)propane – an intramolecular excimer forming probe, as well as perylene and 1,6-diphenylhexatriene – well-established anisotropy probes] also manifest the unprecedented increase in the viscosity of the DA-based DES system upon MEA addition. The carboxylic acid functionality of the DA plays a crucial role in bringing microstructural changes within the system as MEA is added. Physicochemical properties of DES systems can be effectively manipulated by not only changing the constituents and their compositions, but also by judicious addition of a co-solute/co-solvent. This work offers an easy and efficient way to favorably tailor the properties of interest of these environmentally-benign media. Introduction In recent decades, efforts have been invested by the scientific community in creating more cost-effective and environmentally-benign alternatives to conventional solvents that can exhibit novel and tunable solvating capabilities. 1,2 In this regard, deep eutectic solvents (DESs), usually formed from the combination of H-bond donor (HBD) and H-bond acceptor (HBA) moieties, have garnered considerable attention. 3-7 Their physicochemical attributes have been extensively documented in numerous publications in recent times.6-13 An important yet newer subset of the survey involves the exploration of "binary" mixtures, which include DESs as one of the components. Such a mixture consisting of a DES and a small functional molecule can introduce a new complexity to these media and can offer tunability to their existing physicochemical Department of Chemistry, Indian Institute of Technology Delhi, Hauz Khas, New Delhi-110016, India. However, investigations pertaining to these mixtures are rare and less-detailed than those on pure DESs. While the effect of water has been extensively studied experimentally and computationally, 14-19 the interest is now shifting towards the potential offered by a mixture of DES with small organic functionalities. By mixing a DES with a judiciously selected molecule having appropriate functionalities, not only can the physicochemical properties of the DES be tailored effectively but media having unusual properties may be obtained through disturbing/modifying the existing interactions between the HBD and HBA within the system. In this context, the knowledge of molecular-level microstructural transition within such media becomes of utmost importance. The primary objective of this work is to afford the microstructural transition within the "binary" mixtures of naturally-derived hydrophobic DESs (HDESs) and a small organic molecule, ethanolamine (MEA), which is a good H-bond donor as well as acceptor. We have also identified an optimum concentration of MEA, which ensures a maximum water retention by the system. This unu- sual behavior has prompted us to investigate the microstruc- tural transition within these fatty acid-based DESs in the presence of MEA in a comprehensive manner. Towards this end, we have selected three (3) DESs constituted of a saturated alkyl chain fatty acid (n-decanoic acid; DA) and two common terpenes (thymol; Thy and menthol; Men) in a molar ratio of 1:1, namely (DA:Thy), (DA:Men) and (Thy:Men). We investigated the impact of the addition of varying amounts of MEA (up to mole fraction 0.50) on their physicochemical properties. Dynamic viscosity measurements carried out initially within a temperature range 293 to 343 K show an unusual increase in viscosity upon MEA addition to DA-based DESs, whereas the viscosity change in the (Thy:Men) DES was as expected. The (DA:Thy) DES system has shown a more pronounced effect with MEA addition compared to the (DA:Men) and (Thy:Men) systems. Therefore, to obtain insight into the structural transitions, if any, within the MEA-added (DA:Thy) DES system, rheology, electrical conductivity, UV-vis as well as FTIR absorbance, and differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) of this system were investigated. Furthermore, suitable optical spectroscopic probes were employed to obtain empirical Kam-let-Taft parameters of solvent polarity and H-bonding ability, and the microviscosity of the aforementioned systems was explored using a ratiometric intramolecular excimer forming fluorescent probe along with steady-state and time-resolved fluorescence anisotropy probes. This afforded insights into the microfluidity afforded by the MEA-added DES media to solutes of importance and also revealed the correlation between the unusual increase in bulk viscosity with the probe-reported microviscosity within such interesting media. ## 2. Discussion The anomalously high viscosity of terpenoid containing DA-based DESs upon addition of MEA is the most interesting aspect of this work considering no gel-phase is formed as clearly implied by the rheology measurements. The viscosity of the MEA-added DA-based DES systems is observed to even surpass the viscosity of the neat components – DES and MEA – at all the investigated compositions and temperatures, which is a rarely observed phenomenon. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first report documenting such viscosity ‘synergism’ involving DES systems. Similar behavior has primarily been observed in a few non-DES systems previously. For instance, viscosity synergism has been reported for ionic liquids mixed with polymers, such as [emim][OTf] + PEG MMA (6.2 ethoxy units in PEG) and [emim][BF₄] + PEG DMA (9 ethoxy units in PEG) at 40 °C, as well as for [bmim][PF₆] + PEG systems (PEG 200, 400, 600, and 1000) at specific temperatures and compositions.³⁹ Viscosity synergism in aqueous mixtures is reported for short-chain alcohols,⁴⁰ dimethyl sulfoxide,⁴¹ hydroxypropyl-substituted guar and carboxymethyl hydroxypropyl-substituted guar,⁴² acetone,⁴³ and isobutyric acid,⁴⁴ while in non-aqueous systems, it has been observed in only a few systems, such as (methanol + chloroform),⁴⁵ (o-chlorophenol + dioxane),⁴⁶ (carbon tetrachloride + ethyl acMEAte),⁴⁷ (dimethyl sulfoxide + acetic acid),⁴⁶ and (methanol + toluene).⁴⁷ The rarity of viscosity synergism within non-aqueous systems underscores the novelty of the current findings. There are circumstantial pieces of evidence suggesting that even a slight modification in HBD and HBA constituents of DES can result in drastic alteration in their physicochemical proper- ties, and hence, their interactions with other moieties.6,19,48 In the present investigation, drastic alterations are induced by MEA as an additive that significantly perturbs the existing H-bonding network of the DES. Among the major alterations, a pronounced synergistic viscosity effect is observed in long chain fatty acid (i.e., DA) based DESs in contrast to those DESs that do not have carboxylic acid as a constituent. Typically, this trend is observed in H-bonded systems where H-bond strength weakens as the temperature rises. FTIR absorbance data also supports this hypothesis suggesting that extended H-bonding is responsible for the synergistic effect in viscosity. However, based on electrical conductivity and UV-vis absorbance data, it appears that in MEA-added DA-based DESS, the synergistic viscosity effect is not solely due to the formation of an extended H-bonding network, additional factors, such as induced ionic interactions, also contribute significantly in bringing out synergism. Due to the confluence of various factors, the system exhibits a divergence point (χMEA ~ 0.3) beyond which viscosity and electrical conductivity experiences an exponential rise. FTIR absorbance has been highly instrumental in determining the extent of chemical and physical interactions present within the systems; for example, MEA-added (Thy:DA) has much higher chemical activity as compared to MEA-added (Thy:Men). Specifically, physical interactions are evident by subtle changes in the bending and stretching frequencies of various functional groups, such as, C=C, C-O, NH2, -OH, etc., upon addition of MEA. This implies the presence of strong physical interactions, H-bonding in particular. Chemical interactions are strongly detected in the stretching frequency of the carbonyl peak of DA along with the electrical conductivity and UV-vis absorbance data. Additionally, formation of new fluxional bonds or entities is further supported by the strong exothermic events at lower temperatures in the DSC profile of MEA-added DES systems, further supporting the presence of chemical interactions. Interestingly, ratio of excimer-to-monomer emission intensity of BPP and steady-state (perylene) and time-resolved (perylene and DPH) anisotropy measurements suggest that chemically-driven bulk viscosity mirror images the local cybotactic region viscosity (i.e., microviscosity) sensed by the solute probes. The MEA-added (Thy:DA) DES systems exhibit both physicochemical changes and induced ionic interactions that result in higher and unexpected viscosity in comparison to the MEA-added (Thy:Men) DES system, which demonstrates only physical interactions albeit weaker in comparison. ## 5. Conclusion The H-bonding and other interactions within DESs constituted of carboxylic acid as a constituent can be effectively manipulated and altered by addition of a judiciously selected external species. MEA, capable of readily forming H-bonding, when added to (Thy/Men:DA) DESs not only significantly alters the H-bonding network, but also creates induced ionic interactions within the DES system. These major microstructural changes amply get manifested in an anomalous increase in the viscosity and electrical conductivity of the system – both these properties attain unusually high values that are much higher than that of the neat DES and neat MEA. The MEA-added DA-based DESs behave as Newtonian fluids thus discarding the possibility of gel formation within the system. The appearance of color upon MEA addition to DA-based DESs hints at the possible presence of larger aggregates due to H-bonding and induced ionic interactions, which is further supported by significant altera- tions in the IR absorbance bands and the emergence of new bands perhaps due to the formation of fluxional bonds. Solute cybotactic region viscosity (microviscosity) mirrors the bulk dynamic viscosity, further supporting the above reasons for the physicochemical changes within the MEA-added DA-based DES systems. The work put-forth an effective way of modulating the properties of DESs by addition of judiciously selected additives without altering the DES constituents and composi- tion. The outcome widens the application potential of DESs and further enhances their utility as new-age environmentally- benign inexpensive bio-derived solubilizing media.
